titel: Creating Shared Prosperity With AI: Stanford Digital Economy Lab’s Erik Brynjolfsson

einzeiler: How human choices shape the economic impact and future of AI with Erik Brynjolfsson.
kurzfassung: Technology advances rapidly, but human economic institutions and organizations are struggling to keep up with the pace of change. Erik Brynjolfsson discusses the J-curve of productivity, the impact of AI on early-career workers, and why our values and choices matter more than ever. Rather than viewing artificial intelligence as something happening to us, we must actively decide how to use it to create shared prosperity.
stichpunkte: Technology capabilities advance much faster than our economic institutions, skills, and organizational structures.
People often make the mistake of asking what AI will do to us instead of focusing on what we will do with AI.
Self-driving cars took longer to become widespread than initially expected, while language models advanced faster than anticipated.
Economic metrics struggle to capture the value of free digital goods and intangible assets.
Research using payroll data shows a noticeable decline in employment for early-career workers in AI-exposed tasks.
Tasks that augment human skills and create new opportunities show growing employment, unlike those focused purely on automation.
General purpose technologies require complementary investments in intangible assets, leading to a temporary J-curve dip in productivity.
The Turing trap limits our vision by focusing solely on making machines imitate humans rather than augmenting new capabilities.

clips.hook: Political institutions and businesses are not keeping up
clips.text: Human organizations adapt much slower than expected, and productivity growth has not accelerated significantly despite new technological capabilities.

clips.hook: Automated cars have a significantly lower accident rate than humans
clips.text: Autonomous vehicles achieve accident rates ninety percent lower than human drivers, though they occasionally navigate more cautiously and slowly.

clips.hook: Employment declined for young workers in heavily exposed occupations
clips.text: An analysis across hundreds of occupations reveals a notable drop in employment specifically for young professionals facing high AI exposure.

clips.hook: Companies spend billions on training increasingly massive models
clips.text: The immense financial resources required for compute, data, and parameters have escalated model training costs to staggering heights.

clips.hook: Neither blind optimists nor blind pessimists have the right approach
clips.text: Both extreme viewpoints share a fundamental flaw by treating artificial intelligence as an external force rather than recognizing human agency.

beschreibung:
Erik Brynjolfsson has a challenge for anyone worried about artificial
intelligence: Stop asking what AI will do to us, and start asking what
we will do with AI.

In this episode, the Stanford University economist explains why technology isn’t the biggest barrier to progress — people, organizations, and institutions are. Drawing on new research into AI’s impact on jobs, productivity, and economic growth, he argues that the future isn’t predetermined: It will be shaped by the choices we make today. This is a timely conversation about human agency, shared prosperity, and why the most important AI breakthroughs may have less to do with technology than with how we use it. Guest bio: Erik Brynjolfsson is the Jerry Yang and Akiko Yamazaki Professor and senior fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, and
director of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. He is also the Ralph
Landau Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy
Research, professor by courtesy at the Stanford Graduate School of
Business and Stanford Department of Economics, and a research associate
at the National Bureau of Economic Research.

A best-selling author, Brynjolfsson focuses his research on examining the effects of information technologies on business strategy, productivity and performance, digital commerce, and intangible assets.
